Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
I've read it. This report settles more than any of the earlier documents. It also states two of its results more firmly than its own tables support: that the gain declined, and that meetings mediate it. And one detail in its "unplanned observation" changes how the decline should be read.

## What it reports

**Varden case-processing at 24 months.** The trial ran for 24 months, with a second hours measure added: active log-in time on the case-management system. Results relative to control:

| Measure | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |

Quality, sick days (−27%) and resignations hold up.

**Mediation.** The analysis was registered at month 11. Recurring meetings in treated offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours a week, while control offices went from 7.2 to 7.0. The registered model attributes the per-hour gain as follows:

- Meetings: 47% (CI 28 to 66)
- Fatigue: 18% (CI 2 to 34)
- Unexplained: 35%

**Counter arm.** The county ended it at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and restoring service would have needed 12% more staff and raised cost per contact by about 9%.

**Unplanned observation.** At month 15, two control offices audited and cut their own meetings, from 7.1 to 5.0 hours a week. Their output per hour then rose 4.1% against their own previous six months.

**Halden subset.** Of the 23 organisations with records, 14 responded. Three had reverted (hospitality, retail, a marketing agency), with output indices of 88–91 at reversion. The 11 that continued show output at 96.8 and hours down 13.4%, which gives +11.8% per hour. The authors call these survivors twice over.

**Rebuttals of earlier claims.**

- Against "entirely an artifact": Varden meets every standard the re-analysis itself recommended and still shows +8.5%.
- Against "no sign of decay": all four of the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.

I checked the arithmetic:

- Per-hour gains: 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% and 0.966/0.89 = +8.5%.
- Halden subset: hours ratio 34.9/40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8/0.866 = +11.8%.
- Mediation shares sum to 100%.
- Treated meeting time minus control at 24 months is 3.3 hours, matching the month-six cross-section.

## What this settles

**"Entirely an artifact" is refuted.** A randomised trial with record-based output, log-measured hours and two years of follow-up shows a per-hour gain whose interval excludes zero. This is the strongest result in the five documents.

**The meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" has lost its support.** It rested on four studies with exactly the design features the meta-analysis itself found inflate effects. This confirms what I suspected last time, now from the supplementary table rather than by inference.

**Coverage-bound work is closed as a question.** Two years of evidence, an informed decision by the employer, and a costed estimate of what restoring service would take.

**The baseline assumption behind my meeting-hours arithmetic held.** Treated offices started at 7.4 hours of meetings a week and control offices at 7.2. The comparison I made earlier was valid.

## Where the report says more than its data show

**1. "The gain has declined" is a point-estimate difference, not an established decline.**

The like-for-like timesheet estimates are +12.5% (6.9 to 18.4) and +9.8% (4.6 to 15.2). The intervals overlap almost entirely. The body calls this "consistent with some fading", which is accurate. The Summary states it as a finding.

The Summary also says the gain fell "from 12.5% to 8.5%". That compares a timesheet figure at nine months with a log-based figure at 24 months, and so mixes a change in measure with a change over time. Since both estimates come from the same offices, the authors can estimate the change directly with its own interval, and should.

**2. The control offices' meeting audit may account for part of the apparent decline.**

The two control offices that cut meetings raised their own output per hour. That lowers the treated-minus-control gap without anything fading in treated offices. A rough calculation:

- Two of seven control offices, each gaining about 4%, raises the control average by about 1.2 points.
- That applies from month 15 onward.
- It could therefore explain roughly 40% of the 2.7-point drop.

It is also likely that the nine-month report's meetings finding is what prompted the audit. If so, this is spillover caused by the trial itself.

The report presents the audit as a hint about reorganising without cutting hours. It is also contamination of the comparison, and the decline should be re-estimated with those two offices excluded or modelled.

**3. The control meeting figures don't reconcile.**

If two control offices fell to 5.0 hours, a control average of 7.0 at month 24 requires the other five to have risen from about 7.2 to about 7.8 hours. That may be real, but it should be reported. Otherwise one of these figures is measured differently from the other.

**4. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation result.**

The meeting reduction was not randomised. The 47% therefore depends on there being no unmeasured confounding between meetings and output, as the Limitations section acknowledges, though the Summary doesn't reflect it.

There are two further reasons to temper the claim:

- **Too few independent units.** "A larger sample of office-months" still means 7 treated and 7 control offices. If the confidence intervals treat office-months as independent, they are too narrow.
- **Not an independent replication.** The registered test uses the same offices that generated the hypothesis. Registration protects against overfitting the model, but this is a pre-specified test, not a fresh sample.

A fair statement would be that the registered mediation analysis supports meetings as the largest measured pathway.

## What the accounting adds

As I did with the nine-month data, take hours that weren't spent in meetings. Assume control hours stayed at about 37.9 a week, as the nine-month report found.

- Control non-meeting time: about 37.9 − 7.0 = 30.9 hours.
- Treated non-meeting time: about 33.4 − 3.9 = 29.5 hours.
- That is a fall of only about 4.5%, against a 3.4% fall in output.
- Output per non-meeting hour is therefore roughly +1%.

This has two implications.

**What the system logs measure.** If log-in time recorded only active case work, it would exclude meetings. Log hours would then have fallen by about 4.5%, and output per log-hour would be near +1%. The report instead shows logs falling by 11% and output per log-hour rising by 8.5%. So the logs must measure time logged in, including meetings. That matters for how to read the mediation result: meeting cuts raise output per log-hour mainly by removing hours that produce no cases, not by making case work faster. The report should say which of these the logs measure.

**How big the meetings share is.** On this accounting, nearly all of the per-hour gain is time removed from meetings. The mediation model credits meetings with 47%. The two answer different questions. The accounting assumes meetings produced nothing, while mediation estimates a statistical association. The gap between them is worth reconciling: it bears directly on whether fatigue and the unexplained 35% are as large as Table 2 suggests.

## Smaller points

- **One reverting Halden organisation doesn't fit the coverage/discretionary split.** The marketing agency cited client deadlines, and the meta-analysis would code marketing as discretionary. Work paced by clients' deadlines may be a third category: no requirement to be present, but no freedom over timing either.
- **"Upper bound" for the Halden subset is too formal.** With no comparison group, secular trends could push the estimate either way. "Likely optimistic" is accurate.
- **The 9-of-23 non-response is undescribed.** The nine Halden organisations that didn't provide data aren't characterised. If they are disproportionately ones that reverted, the 3-of-14 reversion rate understates reversion.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Status | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Settled** | Coverage-bound work: reduced hours reduce output and service, and restoring service costs about 9% more per contact. |
| **Settled** | The gains in uncontrolled pilots are inflated. The per-hour gain is not entirely an artifact. |
| **Well supported** | Discretionary work: output per hour up about 8.5–10% at two years in a randomised trial. Output per worker slightly below control (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2). |
| **Supported, with caveats** | Cutting recurring meetings is the largest measured pathway. The accounting suggests it may be most of the gain. |
| **Open** | Whether the gain is fading, given that the estimated decline is within noise and partly confounded by the control offices' audit. |
| **Open, and now the key question** | Whether reorganisation without cutting hours captures most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes it happen and last. Only a trial with a reorganise-only arm can answer it. |

The last row is now the most useful practical question. It suggests a three-arm trial: reorganisation only, hours cut only, and both together. I can sketch that design, write a referee report on this follow-up, or consolidate the five documents into one synthesis note.
